# Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs

Ruisheng Sun    Jiaqi Shao    Weijia Han    Linxi Ju    Yunzhen Zhang
Affiliation: Binyan Sun, Rong Chen, Ye Lu, Rui Hu, Bing Luo
Affiliation: Duke Kunshan University & Duke University
Affiliation: Benjamin Blas Maristany, Ernesto Escobar Affiliation: Duke
University

###### Abstract

Traditional interactive narrative systems offer strong authorial control
and structural coherence but often restrict player agency. In contrast,
LLM-driven narratives enable open-ended generation and greater
flexibility, yet frequently suffer from inconsistency and diminished
narrative control. To navigate this trade-off, we propose a hybrid
narrative framework that dynamically balances pre-authored content with
real-time LLM generation via semantic similarity alignment.
Additionally, sustaining narrative quality over extended gameplay
remains a core challenge in LLM-based storytelling. To address this, we
introduce a self-evolving, feedback-driven optimization framework that
leverages in-context learning to iteratively refine prompts, eliminating
the need for manual prompt engineering. Through a case study and
participant-based evaluation, we show that our framework enhances
narrative coherence while preserving player agency, effectively aligning
generated content with both authorial intent and evolving player
behavior.

## 1 Introduction

![Overview of the dynamic narrative generation system. It begins with
pre-generated mode, where authored scripts form structured plots,
progresses to gameplay mode, where the system either selects pre-written
paths or generates new ones, and concludes with a feedback loop that
refines prompts over time, making the system
self-evolving.](2611.01954v1/figs/overview.png)

Figure 1: System Architecture Overview. Our framework addresses
coherence, adaptability, and continual improvement via three
interdependent phases: I. Pre-generated Mode transforms author-defined
Game Scripts into modular Game Plots offline using an LLM Generator,
ensuring narrative structure and quality; II. Gameplay Mode dynamically
selects between pre-authored and generated content using an adaptive
narrative strategy that responds to player choices; and
III. Self-Evolving Optimization uses player feedback to iteratively
refine prompts via an LLM Optimizer, enhancing future generation. These
refined prompts guide the LLM Generator to produce contextually grounded
narratives that reflect both authorial design and player behavior.

For decades, designers of interactive narratives have pursued the dual
goals of crafting compelling, coherent stories and of affording players
agency  ([Domsch, 2013](#bib.bib24); [Tanenbaum and Tanenbaum,
2010](#bib.bib35); [Carstensdottir et al., 2021](#bib.bib27)): the
ability to take meaningful actions that influence the game or story.
Traditional systems based on branching storylines and fixed dialogue
trees provide reliable and well-crafted experiences. However, their
reliance on predefined choices often results in predictable outcomes,
limiting players’ ability to shape the story and reducing the sense of
personal agency.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new capabilities
for interactive narrative systems by generating real-time text and
responsive character behavior ([Andres et al., 2024](#bib.bib23)),
enabling narratives that can dynamically adapt to player input. However,
this flexibility introduces fundamental challenges: LLMs’ inherent
stochasticity and context sensitivity can lead to narrative incoherence,
inconsistent character behavior, and loss of authorial control ([Gu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib44); [Alavi et al., 2024](#bib.bib30)).

Prior work has explored various generation strategies, including
constraining LLM outputs within predefined narrative structures [Sun et
al. (2023)](#bib.bib17); [Earle et al. (2025)](#bib.bib26), while others
focus on personalization [Villareale et al. (2023)](#bib.bib15); [Fu et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib16) and leveraging multi-agent coordination for
long-form generation [Zhang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib13) and
PANGeA [Buongiorno et al. (2024)](#bib.bib12). However, these systems
reveal persistent trade-offs: those prioritizing flexible generation
often suffer from degraded coherence over time [Peng et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib18); [Jeong and Lee (2025)](#bib.bib19). More
critically, they remain fundamentally static in their generation logic,
i.e., their prompts and generation strategies are fixed once designed.
The recent SCORE framework demonstrates that even well-engineered static
prompts cannot maintain quality across extended interactions ([Yi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib6)), highlighting the need for a narrative system
that adapts and improves over time.

To address these limitations, we propose a two-system framework that
progressively builds narrative capabilities:

System 1: Narrative Structure and Adaptive Strategy adaptively decides
between reusing pre-authored content and generating new narrative in
real-time, based on how well player actions align with the intended
story direction. We model the game plot as a hierarchical narrative tree
whose authored nodes form a reusable backbone, while runtime generation
inserts context-constrained branches when player action deviate. This
adaptation is guided by semantic alignment score [Wang et al.
(2020)](#bib.bib9) that quantifies the match between player actions and
narrative context.

System 2: Self-Evolving Optimization enhances System 1 by refining the
prompts used in its narrative generation, which strengthens long-term
coherence and character consistency. It analyzes player feedback across
narrative coherence, NPC consistency, and player agency via
feedback-driven optimization with In-Context Learning (ICL [Madaan et
al. (2023)](#bib.bib2)), thereby diagnosing narrative issues and
refining the prompts that guide System 1’s generation, ultimately
improving storytelling quality at scale without manual prompt
engineering.

We evaluate our approach through a case study based on the “Escape from
Fort Joy” narrative arc [Larian Studios (2017b)](#bib.bib4) from
Divinity: Original Sin 2 [Larian Studios (2017a)](#bib.bib5), showing
that our system maintains narrative coherence while giving players
meaningful choices and automatically improves over time based on player
feedback.

To summarize, our contributions are:

1.  1.  Narrative Structure and Adaptive Strategy: We introduce a modular
        narrative construction framework that transforms pre-authored
        scripts into reusable narrative graphs, together with a semantic
        alignment mechanism that dynamically decides when to follow authored
        branches versus generating context-constrained new content.
2.  2.  LLM-Driven Self-Evolving Optimization: We develop an automated
        feedback-to-improvement system in which our LLM-based Optimizer
        analyzes player feedback, diagnoses narrative issues, and generates
        refined prompts—creating a closed-loop optimization cycle for
        continuous quality improvement (aligning with continual
        human-in-the-loop optimization principles ([Liao et al.,
        2025](#bib.bib25))).
3.  3.  Human-Centered Evaluation and Impact: Our user studies (N=12)
        demonstrate that the system evolves through long-term player
        interaction, balancing authorial control and generative freedom to
        improve coherence and immersion.

We will release our code and the Fort Joy scenario specification to
facilitate reproducibility.

## 2 Related Work

##### Balancing Narrative Coherence and Player Agency

Player agency-the player’s ability to take actions or make choices that
meaningfully shape the narrative [Tanenbaum and Tanenbaum
(2010)](#bib.bib35); [Carstensdottir et al. (2021)](#bib.bib27);
[Cavazza and Young (2017)](#bib.bib28)—has long conflicted with
narrative coherence.Traditional branching structures (e.g., Twine, Ink)
restrict actions [Domsch (2013)](#bib.bib24), while the GFI framework
formalizes narrative via Goals, Feedback, and Interpretation but scales
poorly to unanticipated inputs [Cardona-Rivera et al.
(2020)](#bib.bib29). Even modular frameworks like WhatELSE [Ruan et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib10) require manual specification, fixing coherence at
authoring time. Short’s taxonomy [Short (2016)](#bib.bib1) further shows
rigid branching fails for player-driven progression. In the ICIDS
tradition, Goins ([Goins, 2018](#bib.bib40)) proposes structural
manipulation of space and interactivity as a storytelling model, and
Ferri ([Ferri, 2015](#bib.bib41)) analyzes how narrative structures
operate across IDN authoring systems. Together, these suggest
pre-authored structures alone cannot ensure coherence when player intent
is unpredictable; with LLMs, structural guarantees weaken, motivating
continuous realignment of generative output during gameplay.

##### LLM-Driven Story Generation

LLM assistance in narrative creation spans designer and player
workflows [Green et al. (2018)](#bib.bib32). In designer-facing
workflows, Su et al. ([Su et al., 2024](#bib.bib11)), Wang et al. ([Wang
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22)), and Chen et al. ([Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21)) show that designers leverage LLMs to brainstorm plot
directions but still struggle with controlling tone, pacing, and
adherence to intended narrative themes; generated content becomes
inconsistent across iterations unless designers intervene with explicit
corrective feedback ([Wang and Kreminski, 2025](#bib.bib34)).

For players, Zhang et al. [Zhang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib20) find
multimodal agents can guide actions but drift in longer interactions;
Peng et al. ([Peng et al., 2024](#bib.bib18)) similarly observe that
LLM-driven NPCs produce engaging moment-to-moment dialogue but fail to
track longer-term goals or maintain stable characterization. Wu et
al. [Wu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib43) propose Playwriting-guided Generation
and Plot-based Reflection to improve structure and alignment, while Wang
et al. [Wang et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib14) help interpret fragmented
narratives. Yet the SCORE framework ([Yi et al., 2025](#bib.bib6))
quantifies that models frequently violate previously established facts
and causal dependencies even when supplied with long
contexts—demonstrating that static prompt-based control is insufficient
for sustaining coherent narratives over extended play.

## 3 System Design

This section details the technical framework of our dynamic narrative
generation system, which integrates LLMs with structured, author-defined
narrative elements and continuous player feedback, balancing emergent
narrative with coherent, high-quality progression.

### 3.1 System Architecture Overview

As shown in
Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs"),
our architecture combines the reliability of pre-authored content with
the flexibility of real-time generation, while continuously learning
from player interactions. The fundamental insight driving our work is
that effective interactive storytelling requires three distinct but
interconnected capabilities: (1) generating coherent, high-quality
narrative content offline; (2) adapting this content dynamically during
gameplay; and (3) learning from player interactions and improving over
time. We implement these capabilities through three interdependent
phases:

- I.
  Pre-generated Mode addresses the coherence problem: LLMs, while
  creative, can produce inconsistent or low-quality content when
  generating narratives without sufficient context. This phase
  transforms human-authored Game Scripts—which specify the environment,
  NPC traits, decision points, and outcomes—into modular Game Plots
  offline by the LLM Generator
  (§[3.2.1](#S3.SS2.SSS1 "3.2.1 Pre-generated Mode ‣ 3.2 Core Mechanisms and Implementation ‣ 3 System Design ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")),
  ensuring baseline narrative quality and structural coherence.
- II.
  Gameplay Mode addresses the adaptation problem: Static pre-generated
  content cannot respond to the full spectrum of player actions. We
  propose an adaptive strategy that dynamically steers narrative
  progression through content selection and real-time generation
  (§[3.2.2](#S3.SS2.SSS2 "3.2.2 Adaptive Narrative Strategy ‣ 3.2 Core Mechanisms and Implementation ‣ 3 System Design ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")),
  using semantic alignment to determine when to reuse pre-generated
  content versus generating new narratives.
- III.
  Self-Evolving Optimization addresses the learning problem: Traditional
  game development relies on manual iteration cycles that are slow and
  difficult to scale. Our system integrates an LLM Optimizer that
  continuously: a) collects and analyzes individual player feedback and
  actions after each gameplay, b) concludes feedback features for
  improvements, c) refines prompts for the LLM Generator, and d) repeats
  as a loop
  (§[3.2.3](#S3.SS2.SSS3 "3.2.3 Self-Evolving Optimization via Prompt Refinement ‣ 3.2 Core Mechanisms and Implementation ‣ 3 System Design ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")).

The three phases operate as an integrated system: the pre-generated mode
establishes the narrative foundation; the gameplay mode uses this
foundation while collecting player data; and the self-evolving
optimization refines the prompts used in the pre-generated mode, forming
a continuous improvement loop.

In our implementation, the LLM Generator leverages gpt-4o-mini [OpenAI
(2024)](#bib.bib8) to generate and adapt narrative content in both
pre-generated and gameplay modes, responding dynamically to both
authorial design goals and player interactions. To ensure continued
alignment between generated content, authorial intent, and evolving
player behavior, we introduce a self-evolving optimization loop powered
by an LLM Optimizer, instantiated by gemini-2.5-flash [Gemini Team,
Google (2025)](#bib.bib3)¹¹ 1 See
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Model Selection Rationale ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
for the model selection rationale., which iteratively refines prompts
and narrative strategies based on feedback.

### 3.2 Core Mechanisms and Implementation

#### 3.2.1 Pre-generated Mode

The pre-generated mode constructs a coherent narrative space offline,
balancing LLM creativity with quality control and narrative consistency.
Traditional approaches face a fundamental trade-off: highly structured
content (e.g., branching dialogue trees [Akoury et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib7)) provides coherence but limits player agency, while
unstructured generation (e.g., pure LLM improvisation) offers
flexibility but risks narrative inconsistency and quality
degradation [Yi et al. (2025)](#bib.bib6). Our solution is based on
hierarchical narrative decomposition: breaking down complex narratives
into modular, reusable components that can be dynamically composed and
adapted while maintaining overall coherence.

The process begins with human-authored Game Scripts, which capture the
author’s design vision: defining environments, initializing NPCs,
specifying end conditions, and formulating key questions that mark
pivotal decision points. These key questions serve as narrative anchors,
focusing generation on specific transitions rather than unconstrained
text. From each key question, the system generates multiple narrative
paths—each addressing the key question from different perspectives or
character actions—and each path is realized as a sequence of modular
nodes, the fundamental units of story execution. Each node encapsulates
a distinct moment in the game world, containing its environmental state,
active NPCs, triggering conditions, and the guiding key question.
Inspired by the GFI framework [Cardona-Rivera et al. (2020)](#bib.bib29)
and MoPS [Ma et al. (2024)](#bib.bib33), which formalize narrative
design and modular premise synthesis, this structure enables flexible
reuse and dynamic selection for coherent, adaptive player experiences.

The system generates paths and nodes through three complementary prompts
(see
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Prompt Templates ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
for full templates): a System Prompt defines global rules, world
constraints, and narrative guidelines; a Scripted Prompt realizes the
author’s intended storyline to form Scripted Branches (the canonical
backbone); and a Generated Prompt produces Pre-generated
Branches—LLM-generated alternatives that expand narrative flexibility
while maintaining character consistency and thematic alignment.
Together, these prompts populate each node with both branch types,
allowing the system to select between them at runtime based on player
input. See
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Narrative Generation Architecture Details ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
for the full architecture diagram
(Fig. [5](#A1.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ A.1 Three-Prompt Architecture for Path and Node Generation ‣ Appendix A Narrative Generation Architecture Details ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")).

#### 3.2.2 Adaptive Narrative Strategy

During gameplay, the adaptive narrative strategy evaluates semantic
alignment between player input and in-game context to determine the most
appropriate narrative path. Our approach draws on insights from [M. and
N. (2024)](#bib.bib31), which emphasizes tailoring narrative progression
to players’ evolving behaviors. Let $`\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$
denote the embedding of the player’s input and
$`\mathbf{n}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$ the embedding of the $`i`$-th
pre-generated node, both generated using MiniLM-L6-v2 [Wang et al.
(2020)](#bib.bib9). The alignment score is computed via cosine
similarity:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
S(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{n}_{i})=\frac{\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{i}}{\|\mathbf{p}\|\,\|\mathbf{n}_{i}\|},
``` |  |

with $`S\in[-1,1]`$, where $`1`$ indicates perfect alignment and $`-1`$
complete opposition. Based on this score, the system applies three
decisions:

1.  1.
    Freeform Exploration: If
    $`S(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{n}_{i})<\theta_{\text{low}}`$, the system
    allows continued player exploration within the current node.
2.  2.
    Authored Progression: If
    $`S(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{n}_{i})\geq\theta_{\text{high}}`$, the system
    selects the best-matching pre-generated node
    $`j=\arg\max_{i}S(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{n}_{i})`$.
3.  3.
    Emergent Adaptation: If
    $`\theta_{\text{low}}\leq S(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{n}_{i})<\theta_{\text{high}}`$,
    the system generates a new node in real-time, considering scene
    state, NPC traits, and unresolved story elements.

We set $`\theta_{\text{high}}=0.70`$ and $`\theta_{\text{low}}=0.40`$
(§[4](#S4 "4 Experimental Setup ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs"))
to ensure pre-generated narrative selection when input closely aligns
with the expected storyline, while allowing dynamic generation under
player-driven interactions. The full procedure is summarized in
Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix C Semantic Alignment-Based Node Selection Algorithm ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Semantic Alignment-Based Node Selection Algorithm ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")),
and
Fig. [6](#A2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix B Adaptive Narrative Strategy Illustration ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Adaptive Narrative Strategy Illustration ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs"))
illustrates this strategy with a branching example.

#### 3.2.3 Self-Evolving Optimization via Prompt Refinement

While the pre-generated mode and adaptive strategy address coherence and
adaptation within a single playthrough, a critical limitation remains:
once prompts are engineered, they remain static. As our evaluation
shows, even well-designed prompts fail to cover all player
behaviors—coherence degrades, character motivations become
underspecified, and end conditions trigger inconsistently. Manual prompt
engineering cannot scale to address every failure mode observed in
extended play.

To overcome this, we introduce self-evolving optimization, an automated
feedback loop that continuously refines the System, Scripted, and
Generated prompts based on aggregated player feedback. As illustrated in
Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2.3 Self-Evolving Optimization via Prompt Refinement ‣ 3.2 Core Mechanisms and Implementation ‣ 3 System Design ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs"),
this mechanism operates in four iterative steps:

1.  1.
    Feedback Collection: After each playthrough, the system captures
    quantitative ratings (on narrative coherence, NPC consistency,
    player agency) and qualitative comments, along with interaction
    logs.
2.  2.
    Diagnostic Analysis: The LLM Optimizer aggregates feedback and
    identifies recurring issues. E.g.“NPC motivation underspecified in
    the Generated Prompt” or “end conditions too rigid to recognize
    natural player agreement.”
3.  3.
    Targeted Prompt Refinement: For each diagnosed issue, the LLM
    Optimizer proposes a concrete textual patch to the relevant prompt
    (see
    Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Worked Example: Feedback-Driven Optimization ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
    for a worked example with NPC Fane).
4.  4.
    Redeployment and Iteration: The refined prompts are redeployed to
    both pre-generation and gameplay modes, creating a closed-loop
    optimization across rounds of play.

Our optimization leverages In-Context Learning and self-reflective
mechanisms [Madaan et al. (2023)](#bib.bib2): the LLM Optimizer
evaluates its own narrative outputs, derives insights from player
engagement, and stores reflections in memory, which inform subsequent
story generation.
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.2.3 Self-Evolving Optimization via Prompt Refinement ‣ 3.2 Core Mechanisms and Implementation ‣ 3 System Design ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
summarizes this process.

1: Player feedback $`F`$, interaction logs $`L`$, prompts
$`P=\{P_{\text{sys}},P_{\text{scr}},P_{\text{gen}}\}`$

2: Refined prompts $`P^{\prime}`$

3: $`D\leftarrow\textsc{Diagnose}(F,L)`$ $`\triangleright`$ LLM
Optimizer identifies issues

4: $`H\leftarrow\textsc{GenerateHypothesis}(D)`$ $`\triangleright`$
e.g., “NPC motivation underspecified”

5: for each prompt $`P_{i}\in P`$ do

6:   $`\Delta\leftarrow\textsc{ProposeModification}(H,P_{i})`$
$`\triangleright`$ specific textual change

7:   $`P^{\prime}_{i}\leftarrow\textsc{ApplyPatch}(P_{i},\Delta)`$

8: end for

9: Deploy$`(P^{\prime})`$ $`\triangleright`$ to pre-generation and
gameplay modes

10: return $`P^{\prime}`$

Algorithm 1 Feedback-Driven Prompt Refinement

![Refer to caption](2611.01954v1/figs/llm_optimizer.png)

Figure 2: Feedback-driven prompt refinement. (1) Feedback Synthesis:
Players provide ratings (1–5) and qualitative comments on NPC
Consistency, Narrative Coherence, and Player Agency, stored alongside
interaction history. (2) Diagnose Analysis: The LLM Optimizer retrieves
this data to identify issues such as inconsistent NPC behavior,
disconnected narrative flow, or illusory agency. (3) Prompt Refinement:
Refined system, scripted, or generated prompts are produced to resolve
diagnosed issues and improve future narrative generation.

## 4 Experimental Setup

We conducted a controlled user study to evaluate the two systems
introduced in
§[3](#S3 "3 System Design ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs").
Because System 2 builds on System 1, we designed two sequential tracks
with the same 12 participants: Track A isolates System 1 by comparing
our structured Game Plot system against a flat baseline that generates
entire scenes in a single LLM call without modular structure or
end-condition constraints; Track B then isolates System 2 by comparing
the self-evolving (optimized) version of System 1 against its static
(unoptimized) counterpart. Thus, Track A’s structured system serves as
Track B’s static baseline, and both tracks used a within-subject design
with counterbalanced condition order.

### 4.1 Participants

We recruited 12 participants (age 18–36) from our university community,
comprising experienced RPG players (n=10) and professional game
designers (n=2); see
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Demographic Data Collection ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
for details. Each participant completed both tracks in a single session
of approximately 240 minutes, with a one-day break between the two
tracks to minimize carryover effects. Within each track, participants
experienced both conditions in counterbalanced order. With a
within-subject design across two tracks, N=12 provides sufficient
statistical power for detecting medium-to-large effect sizes (Cohen’s
$`d\geq 0.8`$) at $`\alpha=0.05`$. The study received ethics approval
from an institutional review board, and all participants provided
informed consent.

### 4.2 Evaluation Dimensions

Our evaluation targeted both story-level and interaction qualities:
narrative coherence (global logical flow, absence of contradictions),
NPC consistency (persona/voice stability and memory across scenes), and
player agency (perceived influence over narrative direction and
outcomes) ([Harrell and Zhu, 2009](#bib.bib37); [Poivet et al.,
2025](#bib.bib36)). These dimensions jointly assessed whether structure
preserves coherence without sacrificing agency, and whether optimization
increases believability and resilience over time. After each
playthrough, participants completed a survey combining 5-point Likert
scales and free-text responses ([Kaptein et al., 2010](#bib.bib39)).²² 2
To ensure participants focused on their experience rather than technical
implementation, we avoided terms related to system architecture (e.g.,
“key questions,” “node generation”).

### 4.3 Scene Data

We authored a compact narrative arc of nine story scenes spanning the
“Escape from Fort Joy” journey. Each scene was specified as a modular
node with a location, trigger conditions, interactive NPCs, a set of key
questions (k1–k3) anchoring decision points, and a precise end condition
defining when the scene closes. Authorial structure set the *order* and
ending rules, while free-form input and node selection allowed *how*
each step unfolded to vary; key choices propagated across scenes (e.g.,
breaking Ifan’s trust reduced support at Scenes 5 and 7). The full scene
list, summaries, and key questions are provided in
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Scene Descriptions and Key Questions ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
(Table [2](#A7.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Appendix G Scene Descriptions and Key Questions ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")).

### 4.4 Study Procedure

Each participant received a standardized 10-minute orientation,
including a 5-minute free-form tutorial with a non-story-critical NPC in
a separate environment. In each track, participants experienced both
conditions in counterbalanced order. For Track A, participants
experienced both *Structured* and *Flat* variants; for Track B, both
*Optimized* and *Static* variants. After each condition, they completed
a structured survey assessing the key dimensions plus secondary measures
(immersion, robustness to unexpected input, willingness to replay),
concluding with open-ended questions. We systematically logged all
player inputs, system responses, node selection decisions, end-condition
triggers, and survey responses.

### 4.5 Data Analysis

Following an inductive thematic-analysis procedure ([Braun and Clarke,
2006](#bib.bib38)), two researchers independently performed open coding
on survey transcripts and in-game logs, resolved disagreements through
discussion, and iteratively refined provisional themes through
cross-referencing (e.g., aligning Opaque Endings complaints with log
segments showing repeated end-condition checks). Final themes were
operationalized, linked to our quantitative metrics, and illustrated
with representative quotations. The complete thematic map and full
coding procedures are provided in
Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J Thematic Analysis Coding Process ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs").

## 5 Results

Our evaluation yields insights into both the structural benefits of our
narrative architecture and its capacity for self-improvement. We present
findings from the two experimental tracks: Track A examines how
author-guided hierarchical structuring balances coherence with player
agency, and Track B investigates whether optimization improves narrative
quality across multiple playthroughs.

### 5.1 Track A: Evaluating Narrative Structuring for Coherence–Agency Balance

Track A evaluates System 1 by having every participant experience both
the structured and flat systems in counterbalanced order, allowing us to
attribute observed differences to narrative structure alone.

![Refer to caption](2611.01954v1/figs/TrackA_Survey_Results.png)

Figure 3: Track A Survey Results. Compared to the flat system, our
structured system improves narrative coherence (+0.5) and NPC
consistency (+0.5), with only a modest reduction in player agency
(–0.2).

| Metric                     | Flat System | Structured System     |
|----------------------------|-------------|-----------------------|
| Immersion                  | 4.0         | 4.3 ($`\uparrow`$0.3) |
| Handling unexpected inputs | 3.6         | 4.1 ($`\uparrow`$0.5) |
| Willingness to replay      | 3.4         | 3.8 ($`\uparrow`$0.4) |

Table 1: Additional Track A metrics (5-point Likert).

Fig. [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 Track A: Evaluating Narrative Structuring for Coherence–Agency Balance ‣ 5 Results ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
shows that the structured system improves *narrative coherence* (+0.5)
and *NPC consistency* (+0.5) with only a modest decrease in *player
agency* (–0.2), indicating a typical coherence–agency trade-off.

To understand why, we examine thematic feedback. The structured system
reduces Memory Failures (9/12 $`\to`$ 2/12) and increases Consistent
Persona (2/12 $`\to`$ 11/12), while also reducing Opaque Endings (7/12
$`\to`$ 3/12) and increasing Earned Closure (1/12 $`\to`$ 9/12). For
example, one participant noted in the flat system: “There were
definitely moments of inconsistency… After I killed an enemy, I entered
‘he didn’t die, just injured,’ Ifan believed it” (P11), whereas under
the structured system: “When the Red Prince adapted to my unexpected
input of confessing my affection… it was clear that my input matters”
(P11).

While the structured system improves coherence, it also increases Choice
Stagnation (1/12 $`\to`$ 4/12), as one participant noted: “It felt like
I had options, but no matter what I picked the story always returned to
the same ending” (P7). Yet it enhances Semantic Adaptation (1/12 $`\to`$
9/12), reflecting stronger uptake of unusual inputs. Thus, stronger
structure limits certain action-level freedoms but fosters a *relational
agency* grounded in responsiveness to player intentions.
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.1 Track A: Evaluating Narrative Structuring for Coherence–Agency Balance ‣ 5 Results ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
further shows improvements in *immersion* (+0.3), *handling of
unexpected inputs* (+0.5), and *willingness to replay* (+0.4).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 5.2 Track B: Evaluating Optimization for Long-Term Evolution

Track B evaluates System 2 by investigating whether feedback-driven
optimization improves System 1’s narrative quality across playthroughs.
Optimization was applied in rounds: after each round, the LLM Optimizer
processed aggregated feedback and logs to refine prompts, which were
deployed for the next round.

![Refer to caption](2611.01954v1/figs/TrackB_Survey_Results.png)

Figure 4: Self-evolving optimization vs. static baseline (5-point
Likert). Iterative refinement improves coherence and NPC consistency by
+0.3 each and agency by +0.2. Gains accumulate across cycles. Takeaway:
Lightweight player-feedback loops tighten character voice and narrative
logic without retraining.

Fig. [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Track B: Evaluating Optimization for Long-Term Evolution ‣ 5 Results ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
shows that the optimized system improves *narrative coherence* (+0.3),
*NPC consistency* (+0.3), and *player agency* (+0.2). Statistical
analysis (n=12$`\times`$3, within-subjects) revealed significant
improvements: coherence 3.9$`\to`$4.2 ($`p<0.05`$), NPC consistency
4.3$`\to`$4.6 ($`p<0.05`$), and agency 3.3$`\to`$3.5 ($`p<0.1`$). These
consistent gains suggest our optimization addresses multiple aspects
simultaneously. The optimization trend across rounds is illustrated in
Appendix
Fig. [10](#A12.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ L.3 Multi-Round Optimization Overview ‣ Appendix L Additional Results: Narrative Flow Examples ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs").

To understand how optimization achieves these improvements, we examine
thematic feedback. Iterative optimization increased Consistent Persona
(6/12 $`\to`$ 11/12), reduced Opaque Endings (7/12 $`\to`$ 3/12;
$`\downarrow`$57.1%), and increased Earned Closure (1/12 $`\to`$ 9/12).
Participants described NPCs as “alive, sharp, and consistent in tone,”
recalling moments where NPCs remembered earlier choices. For example:
“Fane felt like a real schemer… It felt like I was actually negotiating
with Fane” (P5); and “characters felt like they had actual memories and
personalities that persisted” (P5).

While optimization improves coherence, Scene 7 still looped for
non-canonical companion choices (P7, P11), indicating that end-condition
coverage needs expansion—structural limitations require architectural
improvements beyond prompt refinement. Nevertheless, Semantic Adaptation
increased (1 $`\to`$ 9) and Choice Stagnation dropped (8/12 $`\to`$
2/12), aligning with the +0.2 agency gain ($`p<0.1`$). Thus,
optimization also fosters a more authentic agency grounded in
responsiveness to player intentions.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Example: Eliminating “Opaque Endings” via Optimization.

System 2 resolves Opaque Endings by refining prompt logic to recognize
semantic intent rather than exact phrases (e.g., “I accept your terms”).
In Scene 1, this reduced opaque endings from 7/12 to 3/12
($`\downarrow`$57.1%) and increased earned closure from 1/12 to 9/12.
For example, “I’m in, let’s escape together” now triggers the end
condition. See
Appendix [L.4](#A12.SS4 "L.4 Optimization Workflow: Eliminating Opaque Endings ‣ Appendix L Additional Results: Narrative Flow Examples ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
for the full workflow and comparison.

### 5.3 Discussion

Our study shows that a hybrid architecture combining authorial structure
with feedback-driven optimization effectively manages the
coherence–agency trade-off. System 1 improved coherence (+0.5) and NPC
consistency (+0.5) with only modest agency reduction. Critically, this
trade-off is dynamic: Track B shows that System 2’s optimization
mitigates agency constraints, reducing Choice Stagnation (8/12 $`\to`$
2/12) and increasing Earned Closure across rounds. Rather than zero-sum,
coherence and agency can be reconciled through Emergent Adaptation
(semantic routing) and character-consistent responses in Freeform
Exploration.

Our framework addresses limitations of both static authoring tools
(e.g., Ink³³ 3
[https://www.inklestudios.com/ink/](https://www.inklestudios.com/ink/),
Twine⁴⁴ 4 [https://twinery.org/](https://twinery.org/)) and fully
generative systems (e.g., AI Dungeon⁵⁵ 5
[https://aidungeon.com/](https://aidungeon.com/)): the former cannot
adapt to unforeseen player behaviors during play, while the latter
suffer from narrative drift and inconsistency in extended sessions [Yi
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib6). These challenges highlight the need for
systems that go beyond single-pass generation and instead support
continuous learning and player-informed refinement.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced a self-evolving, LLM-driven narrative system for runtime
adaptation and continual refinement with player engagement. Our system
negotiates between pre-authored and generative content through semantic
alignment, sustaining both coherence and freedom. Empirical results show
that our approach improves coherence and preserves player agency under
long-term play. Our work shifts the focus from one-off narrative
generation to adaptive, player-informed systems that evolve over time,
pointing toward a new direction for sustainable, intelligent narrative
system.

## Limitations

Our semantic alignment mechanism has three limitations. First, cosine
similarity captures lexical overlap but not the speaker’s intended
meaning, so it cannot distinguish refusal from postponement or ironic
agreement when embeddings are similar; this contributes to residual
opaque endings (3/12 in the final optimization round). Second, alignment
thresholds were set heuristically from pilot observations rather than a
principled optimization procedure; different thresholds would shift the
balance between authored progression and emergent adaptation. Third,
embedding similarity is less interpretable than symbolic intent
classification, complicating audits of narrative decisions. Dedicated
intent classification modules—possibly with structured knowledge
representations—would decouple narrative closure from surface lexical
similarity and improve robustness and explainability.

##### Sample and Generalizability.

Our evaluation is based on a pilot study with 12 participants recruited
from a university community, primarily experienced RPG players and game
designers. While the within-subject design provides sufficient
statistical power for detecting medium-to-large effect sizes, the small
sample limits generalizability. We did not collect gender or educational
background due to IRB data minimization requirements. Furthermore, our
study focuses on a single narrative arc (“Escape from Fort Joy”) from
one genre (CRPG-style text-driven narrative).

##### System Constraints.

We use two commercial LLMs via API (GPT-4o Mini for generation, Gemini
2.5 Flash for optimization). This setup imposes several constraints.
Context-window limits restrict the narrative history that can be
maintained; summarization may lose fine-grained details needed for
long-term coherence. API latency ($`\approx`$1.4s for GPT-4o Mini) can
disrupt fast-paced interaction. External APIs also raise reproducibility
concerns, as model updates or deprecations may affect behavior across
runs. Future work could explore locally fine-tuned LLMs, hierarchical
context management, and persistent long-term memory.

##### Evaluation Methodology.

Our mixed-methods evaluation combines Likert ratings with qualitative
thematic analysis, which provides rich insights but also has
limitations. The thematic analysis involved two researchers who resolved
disagreements through discussion; formal inter-rater reliability was not
computed prior to reconciliation. Mapping qualitative themes to
quantitative metrics (e.g., aligning “Opaque Endings” complaints with
end-condition logs) was interpretive rather than algorithmic. Our
evaluation also relies on participant self-report; expert-based
assessment would complement it and help gauge applicability in real game
design and production. Finally, the optimized system was deployed in
rounds rather than in real time during a single session, which prevents
intra-session inconsistency but cannot capture continuous adaptation
dynamics.

## Appendix A Narrative Generation Architecture Details

### A.1 Three-Prompt Architecture for Path and Node Generation

The system generates narrative paths and nodes through a three-prompt
architecture that creates a hierarchical branching structure. Each key
question from the Game Script is processed using three complementary
prompts (see
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Prompt Templates ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
for full templates):

- •
  System Prompt: Defines global rules, world constraints, and narrative
  guidelines.
- •
  Scripted Prompt: Realizes the author’s intended storyline with
  specific character arcs and plot points.
- •
  Generated Prompt: Enables adaptive generation of alternative
  narratives for unexpected player choices.

These prompts work together to create two distinct types of narrative
branches within each node:

- •
  Scripted Branches: Pre-authored progression that forms the canonical
  storyline backbone, ensuring coherence and consistency.
- •
  Pre-generated Branches: LLM-generated alternatives that expand
  narrative flexibility while maintaining character consistency and
  thematic alignment.

By structuring content around modular nodes and hierarchical branching,
the system pre-generates coherent yet flexible narrative content that
enables dynamic adaptation during gameplay while preserving story
integrity.

![Refer to caption](2611.01954v1/figs/pre_generated.png)

Figure 5: Narrative Architecture Overview. In the pre-generated mode,
authors design a Game Script that specifies the environment, NPC traits
and goals, key questions, and ending conditions. This script is used to
construct a Game Plot—a modular, hierarchical narrative structure
comprising two types of branches: Scripted Branches, realized by LLM
Generator using Scripted Prompt, follow the author’s scripts. To support
player-driven variability, the LLM Generator dynamically expands
Pre-generated Branches in response to decision points using Generated
Prompt. A global System Prompt governs overarching narrative rules and
constraints.

## Appendix B Adaptive Narrative Strategy Illustration

Figure [6](#A2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix B Adaptive Narrative Strategy Illustration ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
illustrates the adaptive narrative strategy with an example scene and
branching hierarchy. At each layer, if the player does not reach a key
question (key decision), they remain in the current node (1. Freeform
Exploration). Reaching a key question moves the narrative to the next
layer: either to a best-matching pre-generated node (2. Authored
Progression) or an LLM-generated node (3. Emergent Adaptation). This
balances coherence with controlled variation in narrative.

## Appendix C Semantic Alignment-Based Node Selection Algorithm

Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix C Semantic Alignment-Based Node Selection Algorithm ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
summarizes the full node-selection procedure, including embedding
computation, cosine similarity, and the three-way branching logic
described in
§[3.2.2](#S3.SS2.SSS2 "3.2.2 Adaptive Narrative Strategy ‣ 3.2 Core Mechanisms and Implementation ‣ 3 System Design ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs").

1: Player input $`p`$, scene context $`c`$, pre-generated nodes
$`\{n_{i}\}`$, thresholds $`\theta_{\text{low}},\theta_{\text{high}}`$

2: Selected narrative path

3: $`\mathbf{p}\leftarrow\textsc{MiniLM}(p)`$

4: for each $`n_{i}`$ do

5:   $`\mathbf{n}_{i}\leftarrow\textsc{MiniLM}(n_{i})`$

6:
  $`S(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{n}_{i})\leftarrow\cos(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{n}_{i})`$

7: end for

8: if $`S(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{n}_{i})\geq\theta_{\text{high}}`$ then

9:   $`j\leftarrow\arg\max_{i}S(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{n}_{i})`$

10:   return SelectNode$`(j)`$ $`\triangleright`$ Authored Progression

11: else if
$`\theta_{\text{low}}\leq S(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{n}_{i})<\theta_{\text{high}}`$
then

12:   return GenerateNode$`(p,c)`$ $`\triangleright`$ Emergent
Adaptation

13: else

14:   return StayInNode$`(p)`$ $`\triangleright`$ Freeform Exploration

15: end if

## Appendix D Worked Example: Feedback-Driven Optimization

### D.1 Two-Stage Optimization Cycle

We model the LLM Optimizer as an autonomous agent that employs a
methodology inspired by the ReAct framework [Yao et al.
(2022)](#bib.bib42), which synergizes reasoning and acting to solve
complex tasks. LLM Optimizer operates in a two-stage cycle:

1.  1.
    Diagnostic Analysis (Reasoning): LLM Optimizer first synthesizes raw
    player feedback, which includes quantitative ratings (e.g., on NPC
    consistency) and qualitative comments. By analyzing feedback from
    the entire testing group, it identifies recurring issues. For
    example, if multiple players report that an NPC’s behavior is
    erratic, LLM Optimizer forms a diagnostic hypothesis: “Hypothesis:
    The core motivation for NPC ‘Fane’ is underspecified in his
    Generated Prompt, leading to inconsistent dialogue choices under
    player-driven scenarios.”
2.  2.
    Strategic Refinement (Acting): Based on its diagnosis, LLM Optimizer
    proposes a concrete, targeted modification to the relevant prompt.
    This action is not an abstract refinement but a specific textual
    change. For instance, it might generate the following action:
    “Action: Generate a patch for Fane’s Generated Prompt. ADD the
    constraint: ’Fane is fiercely loyal to his village and will always
    prioritize its safety. His dialogue must reflect this core
    motivation, even if it requires him to be evasive or distrustful of
    the player.”’

We instantiate the LLM Optimizer with gemini-2.5-flash, which generates
refined prompts consumed by the LLM Generator (instantiated with
gpt-4o-mini) in subsequent pre-generation cycles (next round of
gameplay) for updating game plots. This creates one closed-loop
optimization. Repeating those steps, the LLM Generator continuously
learns from player experiences to enhance narrative coherence, character
believability, and player satisfaction.

## Appendix E Prompt Templates

This appendix details the three core prompts used in our narrative
generation system.

### E.1 System Prompt

The System Prompt defines global rules, world constraints, and
overarching narrative guidelines for the LLM Generator. This prompt
governs the overarching narrative rules and constraints that shape our
interactive storytelling system.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.2 Scripted Prompt Design

The Scripted Prompt realizes the author’s intended storyline by
generating the canonical, pre-authored path—the backbone of the
narrative tree. It transforms high-level design intent into executable
narrative content.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.3 Generated Prompt

The Generated Prompt enables the system to create alternative narrative
branches when player input deviates from the pre-authored storyline,
facilitating adaptive storytelling while maintaining coherence. This
prompt is designed to generate a meaningful alternative path in response
to a specific decision point (the "transitioning question").

- •

## Appendix H Model Selection Rationale

This section clarifies our rationale for using two distinct language
models—GPT-4o Mini (OpenAI) and Gemini 2.5 Flash (Google)—for different
modules in our system. Our choice was guided by task-specific strengths,
cost-efficiency, and empirical performance considerations. Both GPT-4o
Mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash are lightweight, cost-effective models
optimized for production-scale deployment, but they differ significantly
in their latency and throughput characteristics. According to OpenRouter
benchmarks⁶⁶ 6 https://openrouter.ai/openai/gpt-4o-mini, GPT-4o Mini has
an end-to-end (E2E) latency of approximately 1.36 seconds and average
throughput of approximately 189 tokens/second. In contrast, Gemini 2.5
Flash exhibits an E2E latency of approximately 2.4 seconds (as reported
via Google AI Studio⁷⁷ 7 https://openrouter.ai/google/gemini-2.5-flash),
with a lower average throughput of approximately 70 tokens/second. Given
these performance characteristics, GPT-4o Mini’s superior latency and
throughput make it highly suitable for interaction-intensive narrative
adaptation tasks where responsiveness and low latency are critical for
maintaining conversational flow and adapting to player choices in near
real-time.

On the LMSYS Chat Arena leaderboard⁸⁸ 8 https://lmarena.ai/leaderboard,
which ranks models based on human pairwise chat preference,
Gemini-2.5-Flash ranks \#52, while GPT-4o-Mini ranks \#102 (among over
300 evaluated LLMs). This ranking suggests that Gemini Flash produces
outputs that are more preferred by humans in structured evaluation
contexts, supporting our use of Gemini Flash for optimization tasks
where clear, structured outputs and consistent behavior over repeated
runs are preferred. The optimizer module benefits from predictable and
deterministic patterns rather than immediate responsiveness, making
Gemini 2.5 Flash’s output stability and human preference ranking
well-matched to this task.

In summary, our decision to use two different models stems from a
design-driven division of labor, not platform preference or vendor
loyalty. Each model is selected for the sub-task where it performs most
effectively: GPT-4o Mini for responsive narrative generation that
requires low latency and frequent interaction, and Gemini 2.5 Flash for
structured optimization operations that benefit from consistent, stable
outputs. This hybrid approach allows us to leverage the unique strengths
of each model while maintaining cost-efficiency and system performance
across both real-time narrative adaptation and batch optimization
processes.

## Appendix I Demographic Data Collection

Our Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval protocol required us to
minimize collection of demographic data to only what was necessary for
the study’s research objectives. As a result, we did not collect gender
or educational background information from participants. This decision
was made to prioritize participant privacy and align with our IRB’s data
minimization principles.

The demographic information we collected included: age range (18–36),
RPG experience level (self-reported experience $`\geq`$3 years), and
weekly gaming hours. These metrics were directly relevant to
understanding participants’ gaming background and their ability to
evaluate interactive narrative systems, while avoiding collection of
potentially sensitive demographic identifiers.

Weekly gaming hours were categorized as follows: Light ($`\leq`$4
hrs/week, n=1), Occasional ($`>4,\leq`$15 hrs/week, n=2), and Frequent
($`>15`$ hrs/week, n=9). Individual participant breakdown:

- •
  Frequent ($`>15`$ hrs/week): P1, P2, P3, P4, P6, P7, P10, P11, P12
  (n=9)
- •
  Occasional ($`>4,\leq`$15 hrs/week): P5, P8 (n=2)
- •
  Light ($`\leq`$4 hrs/week): P9 (n=1)

## Appendix J Thematic Analysis Coding Process

We followed Braun and Clarke’s [Braun and Clarke (2006)](#bib.bib38)
six-phase inductive thematic-analysis procedure. Phase 1
(Familiarization): two researchers independently read all 12 survey
transcripts and in-game logs, noting initial impressions. Phase 2
(Initial Coding): each researcher generated line-by-line codes; the two
coders produced 47 and 52 initial codes respectively. Phase 3 (Searching
for Themes): codes were clustered into provisional themes via affinity
mapping; disagreements were resolved through discussion, and 6 themes
emerged. Phase 4 (Reviewing Themes): themes were refined against the
full dataset and cross-referenced with log traces (e.g., aligning Opaque
Endings complaints with the specific end-condition checks that failed).
Phase 5 (Defining and Naming): each theme was operationalized with a
clear definition and desired direction. Phase 6 (Producing the Report):
representative quotations were selected for each theme, balancing
positive and negative experiences. Prior to reconciliation, inter-coder
agreement was 78% (Cohen’s $`\kappa=0.71`$), indicating substantial
agreement.

|  Theme |  Definition (Desired Direction) |  Representative Quote |
|----|----|----|
| NPC Consistency Dimension |  |  |
|  Memory Failures |  NPC contradicts prior facts or forgets commitments. (Lower is better) |  “There were definitely moments of inconsistency. For example, after I killed an enemy, I entered ’he actually didn’t die, just injured,’ Ifan believed it.” (P11) |
|  Consistent Persona |  NPC maintains tone, goals, and speech patterns. (Higher is better) |  “Fane stayed sly and dark-humored, even when I tried to call his bluff about the brick. It felt like I was actually negotiating with Fane.” (P5) |
| Narrative Coherence Dimension |  |  |
|  Opaque Endings |  Scene fails to close despite player indicating completion. (Lower is better) |  “I have to give a very strictly-formatted input to pass the game.” (P12) |
|  Earned Closure |  Scene ends after deliberate choice + in-world acknowledgment. (Higher is better) |  “When I promised Fane, he said ’Good. Now we move.’—it felt real.” (P10) |
| Player Agency Dimension |  |  |
|  Semantic Adaptation |  Unexpected inputs are meaningfully interpreted and incorporated in-character. (Higher is better) |  “When the Red Prince adapted to my unexpected input of confessing my affection for him. His tone changed …It was a clear instance where it is evident that my input matters.” (P11) |
|  Choice Stagnation |  Choices receive surface acknowledgement but do not alter narrative outcomes. (Lower is better) |  “It felt like I had options, but no matter what I picked the story always returned to the same ending.” (P7) |

Table 3: Complete thematic map. Themes are grouped by evaluation
dimension, with color highlighting for each dimension: NPC Consistency,
Narrative Coherence, and Player Agency. Representative quotes include
both positive and negative experiences.

## Appendix K System Interface and Monitoring Details

### K.1 Player Interface

Our system is implemented as a web-based text interface where
participants interact with the narrative through a chat-based dialogue
system
(Fig. [7](#A11.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ K.1 Player Interface ‣ Appendix K System Interface and Monitoring Details ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")).
The central dialogue area presents location descriptions, NPC
interactions, and player input options, enabling natural-language
conversation. This design allows us to focus on narrative quality and
LLM-driven dialogue, aligning with our research focus on interactive
storytelling and character coherence.

### K.2 Backend Monitoring Dashboard

The backend monitoring dashboard provides real-time visibility into the
system’s three phases:

![Refer to caption](2611.01954v1/figs/backend_monitor.png)

Figure 8: Backend Monitor Dashboard. The interface tracks (Left)

## Appendix L Additional Results: Narrative Flow Examples

### L.1 Narrative Branching at Layer N

Figure [9](#A12.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ L.1 Narrative Branching at Layer N ‣ Appendix L Additional Results: Narrative Flow Examples ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
illustrates the narrative branching at Layer N, demonstrating how the
system selects between a pre-generated node (backbone) and an emergent
node (branch) based on player input. At any given layer, the system
selects either a pre-generated node (the structural backbone) or an
emergent node (a pre-generated branch). Crucially, Emergent Adaptation
(Phase II) is structurally identical to Scripted/Pre-generated Branch
(Phase I): both are synthesized with explicit Key Questions (to keep
generation focused) and End Conditions (to ensure the scene closes and
transitions). In the “Lone Wolf” case, the emergent node handles the
tattoo sub-plot, and once its end condition (acknowledgment of the
secret) is met, it steers the narrative back to the main arc (the deal),
ensuring that agency is respected without breaking the global structure.

![Refer to caption](2611.01954v1/figs/NarrativeBranchingN.png)

Figure 9: Narrative Branching at Layer N. Emergent Adaptation (Phase II)
forms a complete node parallel to Scripted/Pre-generated Branch (Phase
I). The system chooses the path using semantic alignment and, after
executing Emergent Adaptation, returns to the main backbone with updated
state.

### L.2 Freeform Exploration Example

When semantic alignment is low ($`S<\theta_{\text{low}}`$), the system
interprets player intent as exploration rather than progression, pausing
plot advancement while maintaining environmental authenticity.
Table [4](#A12.T4 "Table 4 ‣ L.2 Freeform Exploration Example ‣ Appendix L Additional Results: Narrative Flow Examples ‣ Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs")
compares how the same low-relevance input is handled by the flat system
versus our structured system, demonstrating how coherence is preserved.
````
